title: After the Post-Avant-Garde | The Point Magazine
gist: Sean Tatol argues the art world's avant-garde ended symbolically in 2003 (Colin de Land's death, Andrea Fraser's Untitled), that October's institutional critique was fully absorbed as art-world boilerplate, and that the internet is now killing the 'post-avant-garde' subcultural model of coolness by destroying both scene economics and the novelty premium. His prescription is a 'rehistoricized' art that treats the internet as an archive rather than a trend machine, exemplified by Lutz Bacher's oblique practice and Bill Hayden's Ding Dong.

insights.claim: The New York art world's late-avant-garde framework effectively ended in 2003, marked by the death of dealer Colin de Land and Andrea Fraser's Untitled, a video of the artist having sex with a collector who had pre-agreed to buy an edition of the work.
insights.speaker: Sean Tatol
insights.so_what: Dates the end of the last credible 'critical artist' business model — everything sold as avant-garde since is a revival, not a continuation.

insights.claim: Colin de Land's death ended the 'gentleman dealer' model in which a respected intermediary could translate radical, uncommercial artists to an active collector base, and no subsequent New York gallery has improved on it.
insights.speaker: Sean Tatol
insights.so_what: The scarce input in an art scene is not artists but the intermediary who can finance them; its absence, not taste, is what kills scenes.

insights.claim: Andrea Fraser's Untitled (2003) foreclosed any critical distance between artwork and sale, amounting to a frank admission of selling out and signaling that institutional critique had become impossible at the turn of the century.
insights.speaker: Sean Tatol
insights.so_what: When the most committed critic of a system monetizes the critique itself, the system has fully absorbed its opposition — a pattern that repeats in finance and media.

insights.speaker: Sean Tatol
insights.so_what: A case study in what happens to a practice whose animating antagonism is removed: technical virtuosity survives, relevance does not.

insights.claim: The avant-garde rested on a post-Hegelian utopian teleology in which radical critical art would produce corresponding social change, whether by decommodifying art, abolishing the art/life divide or inciting political revolution.

insights.so_what: Explains why cultural risk capital rotated from galleries to venture: the prestige of the outsider-innovator now attaches to founders, not artists.

insights.claim: By the time the October editors published Art Since 1900 in 2004, their once-insurgent critical language had become the art world's default institutional language, converting late-avant-garde artists from adversaries of the system into its representatives.
insights.speaker: Sean Tatol
insights.so_what: The clearest documented case of a counter-canon completing the capture cycle in under thirty years — watch for the same arc in today's insurgent critical vocabularies.

insights.so_what: When a field replaces judgment with theory, quality signals stop being legible to outsiders and the market defaults to price and PR.

insights.speaker: Sean Tatol
insights.so_what: Gives a timing rule: novelty-based valuation is only defensible until the form becomes a genre, after which quality reasserts itself as the discriminator.

insights.claim: The post-avant-garde replaced critical autonomy with self-conscious operation inside the institutions, treating art scenes as subcultural communities that navigate the art system rather than try to reform or destroy it.
insights.speaker: Sean Tatol
insights.so_what: The dominant operating model of contemporary art since 2003 — knowing it explains why 'critique' claims are now decorative rather than programmatic.

insights.claim: In the post-avant-garde frame, 'coolness' is the socially mediated exercise of judgment within an art culture, marking who is seen by peers as navigating it with flair, unpredictability and an exciting sensibility.
insights.speaker: Sean Tatol
insights.so_what: Reframes 'cool' as a distributed valuation mechanism — the informal ratings agency of a subculture, and the thing the internet is destroying.

insights.claim: Lutz Bacher is the most representative post-avant-garde artist because she built an ambiguous artistic subjectivity into the content itself — adopting a pseudonym in the early 1970s, never revealing her given name, interviewing herself in 1976, and making the twelve-hour Do You Love Me? (1994) out of friends and family discussing her.
insights.speaker: Sean Tatol
insights.so_what: Shows the winning strategy under institutional capture: withhold legibility rather than attack the institution.

insights.claim: Bacher treated the art world as a set of expectations to be played with rather than institutions to be overturned, setting stakes that were smaller and more feasible — personal freedom inside the system plus work that excites its audience.
insights.speaker: Sean Tatol
insights.so_what: The realistic alternative to both capitulation and futile critique; the same posture applies to operators inside any captured system.

insights.claim: An art world built on practices like Bacher's is structurally fragile: it must be uncommercial and opaque enough to sustain an insider grammar of reference while still finding money, which depends on exceptional business-side personalities like de Land.
insights.speaker: Sean Tatol
insights.so_what: Identifies single-point-of-failure risk in scene economics — patronage is personality-dependent and does not survive its patrons.

insights.claim: The post-avant-garde rests on three assumptions the internet destroys: that new styles reliably appear each year, that a stable art market stays interested in the subcultural ecosystem, and that enough historical knowledge exists to tell genuine novelty from rehash.
insights.speaker: Sean Tatol
insights.so_what: A checklist for whether any taste-driven market can still generate scarcity value; failing all three collapses the novelty premium.
insights.quote: The internet upends all three of these assumptions.

insights.claim: By making all past media accessible as an archive of free-floating aesthetic signifiers, the internet lets historical content be recycled in an endless simulacrum of ostensibly novel media.
insights.speaker: Sean Tatol
insights.so_what: Novelty becomes unverifiable, so pricing on 'newness' stops working and authentication shifts to provenance and personality.

insights.claim: Anna Weyant's polished imitations of John Currin took her from relative obscurity to Gagosian in 2022 and to auction prices above one million dollars while she was in her twenties and publicly dating the gallery's owner — the archetype of PR-conjured careers replacing subcultural validation.
insights.speaker: Sean Tatol
insights.so_what: A named case of speculative, relationship-driven price formation; a marker for the top of a forced-enthusiasm market cycle.

insights.claim: Social media turns cultural trends into bids for virality and mass attention, making them contrived and commodified in advance by the logic of the algorithm.
insights.speaker: Sean Tatol
insights.so_what: Explains why organic subcultural signal no longer precedes commercial adoption — the funnel has been inverted.

insights.claim: The most well-respected artists in the current New York scene, many in or nearing their forties, are marginal in market terms, and they were the last generation to have formative experiences inside a cohesive scene in the 2000s and 2010s.
insights.speaker: Sean Tatol
insights.so_what: Critical esteem and market value have fully decoupled at the high-quality end — a divergence that usually precedes either repricing or institutional abandonment.

insights.claim: Gen Z artists have traded subcultural credibility for instrumentalized careerism because social media reduced the social to the self-promotional, making selling out a presumed condition of working at all rather than a threat to work around.
insights.speaker: Sean Tatol
insights.so_what: The supply of artists optimizing for distribution over peer validation implies more homogeneous, more sellable, less durable product.

insights.speaker: Sean Tatol
insights.so_what: Patronage risk appetite, not talent, is the binding constraint on cultural production — watch collector behavior, not artist output.

insights.claim: The internet is the larger threat to in-person artistic communities because those communities sustained art precisely by developing semi-autonomous criteria for what counts as cool within them, and when Instagram-friendly figurative painting sells easily the market stops caring about subcultures — after which the subcultures stop caring about themselves.
insights.speaker: Sean Tatol
insights.so_what: Autonomous local standard-setting is the asset being destroyed; its loss removes the filter that produced investable cultural scarcity.
insights.quote: When the art market can get by with flashy and ineffectual figurative paintings that are easy to sell on Instagram, it no longer has any reason to care about what’s going on in artistic subcultures.

insights.claim: The post-avant-garde's core weakness was conflating newness with presentness, an equation that becomes untenable once TikTok and Instagram Reels supply a constant stream of up-to-the-moment new media.
insights.speaker: Sean Tatol
insights.so_what: When novelty is infinitely abundant it is worthless as a value criterion; whatever replaces it is where future cultural pricing power sits.

insights.claim: It may be worth celebrating that the internet has killed art's faith in the progressive periodization of styles, because decoupling art from progress frees taste to become more catholic.
insights.speaker: Sean Tatol
insights.so_what: An explicitly optimistic read on a development everyone else treats as decline — the contrarian position in the culture-decline debate.

insights.claim: Late works by Francis Picabia, Philip Guston and Willem de Kooning were dismissed in their own time as washed-up and out of step — Picabia and Guston for turning figurative, de Kooning for staying loyal to Abstract Expressionism — yet are now seen as reliably great, proving contemporaneity is a poor quality filter.
insights.speaker: Sean Tatol
insights.so_what: Historical evidence that consensus timing judgments misprice durable work — the case for buying critically unfashionable quality.

insights.claim: The internet constitutes an epistemic break on the order of the Renaissance rediscovery of classical culture and the invention of the printing press, and for the arts it can act as a radical reorientation of temporality rather than only as brain-frying and doomscrolling.
insights.speaker: Sean Tatol
insights.so_what: Frames the internet as a supply shock in access to the past rather than only a distribution shock — a different investment thesis about where cultural value forms.

insights.claim: Art's actual function is not to produce newness or directly change the world but to preserve the phenomena of the past — the intangible fabric of lived experience — as a document of the particularity of its own moment.
insights.speaker: Sean Tatol
insights.so_what: A replacement valuation criterion for cultural assets: adequacy to its own moment, not novelty, is what makes work durable.
insights.locator: Instead, the history of art reveals its purpose

insights.claim: The rehistoricized artist stays contemporary while forging a relationship to an open field of influence unhemmed by Western canons — Shakespeare alongside Cao Xueqin, Michael Asher alongside Antonello da Messina, African masks, Angkor Wat, Aboriginal art, Laozi, Montaigne, Beethoven, Pandit Pran Nath, Buster Keaton, Straub-Huillet and Duras.
insights.speaker: Sean Tatol
insights.so_what: The prescribed strategy is archive arbitrage: value accrues to whoever does the historical work competitors skip.

insights.claim: Bill Hayden's show Ding Dong at Gandt in Astoria — six ink-and-wax drawings on freestanding cables including dinosaur eggs, a distorted map of Europe, a Chardin-like still life and a cartoon weed leaf carrying a cross — exemplifies the new paradigm because its studied incoherence belongs indefinably to the present without aspiring to be new or old.
insights.speaker: Sean Tatol
insights.so_what: A concrete, checkable specimen of the thesis; useful as a template for spotting the same move elsewhere before it is priced.
insights.locator: Bill Hayden’s show at Gandt last May

insights.claim: Our experience of a great artwork's persisting vitality is a recognition that it was adequate to the consciousness of its own time, which is why art is needed most now that everything feels unnecessary and interchangeable.
insights.speaker: Sean Tatol
insights.so_what: Names the scarce good in an age of infinite content: specificity that is adequate to its moment, which is precisely what algorithmic production cannot supply.
insights.quote: Only art can make us see our world with fresh eyes.
